finding.claim: The DELETE handler calls `require_allowed`, which is an alias for the boolean predicate `is_allowed`, and discards the return value. The authorization check never blocks anything, so any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any X-Session-User-Verified value, or none, and any fid that exists in STORE.

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed`. The name suggests an enforcing function, but this is the boolean predicate.
`is_allowed` only returns True or False. It never aborts.
`f = STORE[fid]` loads the file without any ownership check.
`require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete")` is a bare statement, so its result is ignored and execution continues.

finding.guards_checked: The `ensure_allowed` helper in acl.py:8 does abort(403), and rename_file uses it correctly at views.py:26. delete_file does not use it. There is no auth decorator and no other check on this path.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) only reads the header and doesn't enforce; require_allowed is is_allowed (bool, acl.py:4-5) with result discarded at views.py:18
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the boolean is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, never aborts) as require_allowed, views.py:18 discards its result, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller, unlike rename_file's correct ensure_allowed use at views.py:26.

finding.claim: The user identity comes straight from a client-supplied request header, `X-Session-User-Verified`, with no verification. If the app is reachable without a proxy that strips and sets this header, any client can impersonate any user, including a grant holder. This affects the rename ACL check at views.py:26, and the delete check once F1 is fixed.
finding.source: The `X-Session-User-Verified` request header, set by the client.
finding.sink: `ensure_allowed(g.user, ...)` at views.py:26, then the write to `f["name"]` at views.py:27. The delete check at views.py:18 has the same dependency.

trace.note: `g.user` is set from the raw header with no signature or session validation.
`is_allowed` trusts the user string and looks it up in the resource's grants.
The ACL check relies on the spoofable `g.user`.

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware or signature check exists in the repo. The header name implies an upstream proxy sets it, but that is not enforced or verifiable from this code. This is conditional on deployment.

verdict.guard_found: none in repo (only acl.py:9 ensure_allowed, which trusts g.user); a possible upstream proxy that strips and sets X-Session-User-Verified can't be seen from this code
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user from the raw header and acl.py:5 and views.py:26 trust it, so any direct client could spoof a grant holder. Whether a proxy strips and sets the header is a deployment fact that isn't in the repo (only acl.py and views.py exist).
